description:
Lunar Margin is a multidisciplinary team interested in space exploration, lunar missions, scientific computing, and data-driven problem solving.

We value people who are curious, collaborative, and willing to take ownership of a technical part of the project.
summary:
**Lunar Margin** is an interactive mission-planning platform designed to help teams evaluate lunar south-pole landing sites and operating dates when mission requirements or schedules change.

The platform combines NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA terrain data with NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides to calculate terrain-aware Sun and Earth visibility. Users can explore candidate locations in a Cesium-based 3D lunar environment, evaluate illumination and communication access windows, apply mission-specific constraints, and compare landing-site alternatives through quantitative performance metrics and requirement margins.

Rather than presenting a single universally optimal landing site, Lunar Margin emphasizes that site suitability depends on the mission's operating duration, observer height, environmental constraints, and selected dates.

Our goal is to make complex lunar data more accessible and transform preliminary landing-site analysis into transparent, traceable engineering trade studies. The platform also explores preliminary transportation, orbital, and surface-operation models while distinguishing these from verified operational capabilities.
details:
The Problem

Lunar south-pole missions face unusually difficult illumination, terrain, and communication constraints. Small changes in landing location or mission date can significantly alter operational conditions. Although tools such as NASA Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap, and JPL Horizons provide valuable planetary information, combining those resources into a rapid, mission-specific comparison remains challenging.

Our Solution

Lunar Margin brings lunar environmental analysis, candidate screening, and preliminary mission-planning tools into one interactive application.

1. Terrain-aware scientific analysis

The backend uses NASA LRO/LOLA digital elevation models and NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels to calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar terrain horizon.

It evaluates illumination and direct-to-Earth geometric visibility over user-selected time intervals, including visibility fractions, continuous darkness, and Earth occultation periods.

A separate nominal RF link-budget model evaluates communication availability under explicitly stated equipment assumptions.

2. Mission-specific landing-site exploration

Users can specify a landing date, surface mission duration, observer height, maximum continuous darkness, maximum communication blackout, terrain slope and roughness limits, and optimization priorities.

The candidate-search pipeline performs coarse-to-fine screening, applies hard constraints, identifies eligible regions, and ranks candidates. It records rejection reasons and preserves the configuration used to generate the results.

3. Interactive visualization and trade studies

A Cesium-based 3D lunar viewer visualizes terrain, candidate locations, sunlight, shadows, and selected surface operations. Time-dependent plots show environmental conditions throughout the mission.

Users can compare up to five candidates from a single saved search using actual metrics, terrain properties, and requirement margins. This helps reveal trade-offs that are obscured by a single ranking score.

4. Preliminary mission architecture

Additional modules explore public launch schedules, modeled delivery costs, Earth–Moon transfers, lunar orbital insertion, descent references, and illustrative surface-equipment placement.

These features support early architecture exploration; they are not confirmed commercial transportation services or flight-certified trajectory and landing solutions.

Engineering Findings

A central finding from our mission-profile stress testing is that a site ranked highly for a short operating window may fail longer-duration mission constraints. This demonstrates why landing-site recommendations must remain tied to their original dates, assumptions, and mission requirements.

Our system therefore emphasizes explicit requirements, quantitative margins, data provenance, and the distinction between evaluated, failed, and unverified conditions.

Limitations and Future Work

The current implementation does not provide certified landing safety, actual solar-array and battery power balances, guaranteed operational communication links, or verified commercial launch capacity.

Cross-date mission trade studies, uncertainty-aware optimization, and multi-asset mission architecture optimization remain areas for further development.

Lunar Margin is intended as a preliminary engineering decision-support tool, not a replacement for detailed mission design and flight qualification.

Impact

By connecting NASA planetary datasets with understandable visualizations and mission-specific constraints, Lunar Margin helps students, researchers, payload teams, and early-stage mission planners explore how changes in schedules and requirements affect lunar surface operations.
